Decision tool for service operators

Does the vendor rate actually save you money?

Compare your current cost with supplier discounts, subcontractor rates, or equipment leases at the job volume you really expect.

Is switching vendors worth it? · This calculator vs. Crest Capital's lease calculator · This calculator vs. comparing the quoted rates by eye

Your current operation

Best at this volumeEnter costs below
OptionMonthly costCost / jobSavings / jobProfit / jobMarginBreak-even

Break-even is an estimate based only on the fixed and per-job costs you enter. Profit and margin use the revenue per job you enter above; review contracts, taxes, fuel, minimums, and service quality separately.

Common questions

Why does one scenario break even at zero jobs and another need four?

Break-even only exists when a scenario charges a fixed fee the baseline does not. In the built-in example, the bulk supplier adds a $100/month fee but drops the per-job cost from $120 to $90 — a $30/job saving, so it takes ceil($100 ÷ $30) = 4 jobs before that fee is paid back. The subcontractor scenario has no fixed fee at all, only a $5/job saving, so there is nothing to recoup and it shows as cheaper starting from job one.

What does “Not cheaper” mean in the break-even column?

It means the scenario loses on both numbers: its per-job cost is higher than your current variable cost and its fixed cost is the same or higher, so no volume of jobs ever makes it win — there is no break-even point to reach, not just a distant one. Compare the “Cost / job” and “Savings / job” columns for that row: a negative savings figure is why.

What does “Below N jobs/mo” mean?

The opposite trade from a fixed-fee break-even: this scenario has a lower fixed cost than your baseline but a higher per-job cost, so it wins at low volume on the fixed-cost saving alone and loses that lead once enough jobs push the higher per-job rate past it. It is cheaper only while your monthly job count stays below the number shown — run more jobs than that and the current operation (or a scenario with a lower per-job cost) wins instead. A no-minimum, pay-per-job vendor compared against a leased or subscription-priced one is the usual shape of this case.

Why enter fixed cost and per-job cost separately instead of one blended rate?

Because they behave differently as volume changes. A monthly minimum or lease payment (fixed) gets cheaper per job the more jobs you run; a per-unit supplier price or mileage rate (variable) does not move with volume at all. Blending them into one number hides which lever actually changes if your job count changes next quarter.

At the default 20 jobs/month, which option actually wins?

The bulk supplier: $1,900/month total versus the current $2,400, for a cost of $95 per job against a $120 baseline — a $25/job saving even after the $100 fixed fee. The subcontractor option is cheaper per job than today but not as cheap as the bulk supplier at this volume, which is exactly why the table ranks all three rather than only showing yes/no.

Is my vendor pricing uploaded anywhere?

No. The comparison runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server. “Save draft” writes your scenarios to this browser's local storage and restores them the next time you open the page, “Copy share link” encodes the same fields into the page's URL fragment so you can hand the comparison to someone else, and the optional usage counter records only which buttons were used, never your rates or volumes.

is-switching-vendors-worth-it.html.text:
← Vendor rate break-even calculator

Is switching vendors worth it?

A supplier discount, a subcontractor rate, or an equipment lease often comes with a fixed monthly fee attached to a lower per-job price. Whether that trade is worth it depends entirely on your actual job volume — the same rate card can be a clear win at 30 jobs a month and a loss at 3.

Open the free vendor rate break-even calculator

What a headline discount cannot see

Fixed fees hide at low volume. A vendor's monthly minimum or lease payment is spread across however many jobs you actually run — fewer jobs means a bigger slice of that fee lands on each one.

Break-even is a job count, not a percentage. The real question is not "is this rate lower," it's "how many jobs a month do I need to run before this rate is lower for me."

Some deals never pay off. If the new per-job cost is not actually lower than your current one, stacking a fixed fee on top makes every volume worse, not just low volume.

A number you can defend

  1. Enter your current jobs per month, revenue per job, current fixed monthly cost, and current variable cost per job.
  2. Enter up to three vendor alternatives as a fixed monthly cost and a variable cost per job.
  3. Compare monthly cost and cost per job at your real volume, not a rate card's advertised number.
  4. Check the break-even job count — the volume where the new fixed cost is paid for by the per-job savings.

Worked example

At 20 jobs a month with no fixed cost, a $120 per-job variable cost is $120 per job. A "Bulk supplier" offer adds a $100 monthly minimum but drops the per-job cost to $90 — $95 per job at 20 jobs a month, a $25-per-job saving worth $500 a month. That $100 minimum pays for itself at just 4 jobs a month, well under the 20 actually run. A "Subcontractor" alternative with no minimum and a flat $115 per job is already cheaper than the $120 baseline at any volume at all, with no break-even threshold to clear.

Common questions

How do I know if switching vendors is worth it?

Compare the total monthly cost at your actual job volume, not the headline per-job rate. A vendor's fixed monthly fee plus its per-job cost, divided by your monthly jobs, gives a true cost per job you can compare directly against your current cost per job.

When does a vendor's monthly minimum pay for itself?

Break-even volume is the new fixed cost minus your current fixed cost, divided by the per-job savings the new rate offers. A $100 monthly minimum against a $30-per-job saving pays for itself at 4 jobs a month; below that volume the fixed fee costs more than the discount saves.

What if the new vendor's per-job rate isn't actually lower?

If the new variable cost per job is equal to or higher than your current one, no volume makes the switch pay off — the calculator reports it as 'not cheaper' rather than a break-even job count, because adding a fixed fee on top of an equal or higher per-job rate never turns a profit at any volume.

vs-comparing-rates-by-eye.html.text:
← Vendor Rate Break-Even Calculator

This calculator vs. comparing the quoted rates by eye

Two rate cards side by side make the lower per-job number look like the obvious pick. It isn't, once a monthly minimum is attached to one of them — the pick depends on how many jobs you actually run.

What comparing rates by eye does

The fast way to size up a vendor switch is to put the two per-job numbers next to each other: your current cost, and the new rate on the quote or rate card in front of you. Whichever number is lower reads as the better deal, and the gap between them reads as the savings.

That works as long as both numbers are the whole cost. It stops working the moment one of them carries a fixed monthly cost the other doesn't -- a minimum order fee, a subscription, a lease payment -- because a fixed cost spread over your actual job volume changes the real per-job number, and by a different amount depending on how many jobs you run.

What this calculator does instead

It takes your current jobs per month, your current fixed and variable cost, and up to three alternatives as a fixed monthly cost plus a variable cost per job -- the same numbers already on the rate card, just entered in full instead of read off the headline. It computes total monthly cost and true cost per job for each option at your own volume, and the exact job count where a new fixed fee stops costing more than its per-job saving returns.

What comparing rates by eye doesWhat this calculator does instead
Compares the per-job number alone, so a quote's fixed monthly cost never enters the comparison. Adds the fixed cost into total monthly cost, so it is counted whether or not it's the headline number.
Gives one answer regardless of volume -- the lower rate "wins" the same way at 3 jobs a month or 30. Reports the job count where a fixed fee is paid back by its per-job saving, so the answer can flip with volume.
Has no way to say a deal is cheaper only up to a point, or never, once a fixed cost runs the other direction. Reports both shapes: a break-even job count, or the volume a saving-on-fixed-cost deal stays cheaper up to.
Stops at cost. A cheaper rate and more profit are treated as the same question. Reports profit per job, monthly profit, and margin at your actual revenue per job for every option, since a lower cost is not always more profit once volume is fixed.
Compares two rate cards at a time, by hand, with no record of the comparison. Compares your current cost against up to three alternatives side by side, with a share link that hands the same numbers to a partner or the vendor.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it runs entirely in your browser, and a share link carries only the numbers in the form -- nothing is uploaded.

Same two rate cards, opposite answer

Take this calculator's own default comparison: a current cost of $120 per job with no fixed fee, against a bulk supplier quoting $90 per job plus a $100 monthly minimum. Read as two rate cards, $90 beats $120 by $30 a job, every time, at any volume.

Run the numbers at 3 jobs a month: the current vendor costs $360, and the bulk supplier costs $370 — ten dollars more, not thirty dollars less, because the $100 minimum outweighs three jobs' worth of $30 savings. At 4 jobs a month, the calculator's own break-even point, the bulk supplier is already $20 cheaper ($460 vs. $480), and at 20 jobs a month the same bulk supplier saves $500 a month ($1,900 vs. $2,400). The rate cards never changed. Only the volume did.

Common questions

What's wrong with just comparing the two rates side by side?

A per-job rate alone leaves out any fixed monthly cost attached to it -- a minimum order fee, a subscription, a lease payment. Two rate cards showing $90/job and $120/job look like a clear $30/job win for the first, but if the $90 rate carries a $100 monthly minimum and the $120 one does not, the comparison that matters is total monthly cost at your actual volume, not the per-job number alone.

How wrong can eyeballing the rate get, in practice?

Using this calculator's own defaults -- a current cost of $120/job with no fixed fee, against a bulk supplier quoting $90/job plus a $100 monthly minimum -- the crossover is 4 jobs a month. Below that, the $100 minimum costs more than the $30/job saving returns: at 3 jobs a month the current vendor costs $360 and the bulk supplier costs $370, ten dollars more overall, despite its rate looking $30/job cheaper on the card. At 20 jobs a month the same bulk supplier saves $500. Same two rate cards, opposite answer, depending only on volume.

Does a higher quoted rate ever still win?

Only through a lower fixed cost, and only up to a volume where that saving runs out -- this calculator reports that case as a job count the deal stays cheaper up to, the mirror image of a break-even count. If the new per-job rate is equal to or higher than your current one with no offsetting fixed-cost saving, no volume makes it worth it, and eyeballing the rate alone cannot tell you which case you are in.

Do I need my accountant's numbers to use this?

No. Four numbers you already have: your jobs per month, your current fixed and variable cost, and the new rate's fixed and variable cost from the quote in front of you. The calculator does the break-even arithmetic; nothing is uploaded, and a share link carries only the numbers you entered.

vs-crest-capital.html.text:
← Vendor Rate Break-Even Calculator

This calculator vs. Crest Capital's lease calculator

One prices a lease in isolation. The other compares whatever rate you were offered — lease, discount, or subcontractor — against what you already pay, at the job volume you actually run.

What Crest Capital's calculator is

Crest Capital is a national equipment financing and leasing lender, founded in 1989 and headquartered in Alpharetta, Georgia, that finances equipment, vehicles, and software for small and mid-size businesses. Its site offers a free calculator that takes the cost of one piece of equipment and estimates the monthly payment for financing or leasing it through Crest Capital, typically as a first step toward submitting an application. It prices one thing — a new lease or loan on one asset — and is built to lead toward Crest Capital's own financing product.

What this calculator is

This page does not estimate a lease payment and is not tied to any lender. It starts from a rate you already have — a supplier's bulk-discount pricing, a subcontractor's day rate, or a lease payment quoted by Crest Capital or anyone else — and compares it against your current fixed and per-job costs at the number of jobs you actually run each month. It shows the monthly cost, cost per job, profit per job, and margin for each option side by side, plus the exact job volume where a new fixed fee pays for itself against the per-job savings it offers. Everything runs in the browser; nothing is uploaded, and there is no application to submit.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I want to finance or lease a new piece of equipment and need a monthly payment estimate before applying. Crest Capital's calculator or a comparable lender's — pricing new financing is exactly its job, and this calculator has no financing terms of its own to offer.
I already have a lease quote, a supplier discount, or a subcontractor rate and want to know if it actually beats what I pay today at my real job volume. This calculator — enter your current cost and the new rate's fixed and per-job figures, and it shows the break-even volume and the cost per job at your own numbers.
I want to compare up to three vendor offers against each other and against my current baseline in one table. This calculator — Crest Capital's tool prices one lease at a time and does not compare it to a baseline or to other vendors.
I don't want to enter my equipment cost into a lender's site before I know whether the deal is worth pursuing. This calculator — it needs only the fixed and per-job cost figures already on the rate card or lease quote, and sends nothing to Crest Capital or anyone else.

Neither tool replaces the other. A business financing a new asset for the first time still needs a lender's own payment estimate — that is what Crest Capital's calculator, or a comparable lender's, is for. Once a rate is on the table, from a lender, a supplier, or a subcontractor, this page is where you check whether it is actually cheaper at the volume you run, before signing anything.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Crest Capital's lease calculator?

They answer different questions. Crest Capital, a national equipment financing and leasing lender founded in 1989 and headquartered in Alpharetta, Georgia, offers a calculator on its own site that estimates the monthly payment for financing or leasing one piece of equipment, vehicle, or software — a first step toward applying for that financing through Crest Capital. This calculator does not estimate a lease payment at all: it takes a fixed cost and a per-job cost for up to three alternatives — a supplier discount, a subcontractor rate, or a lease payment you already have a quote for — and compares each against what you pay today, at your actual jobs per month, to show the true cost per job, the profit and margin at that volume, and the exact job count where a fixed fee pays for itself. If you need a payment estimate for financing new equipment, Crest Capital's calculator or a comparable lender's is built for that. If you already have a rate, a discount offer, or a lease quote in hand and want to know whether it is actually cheaper at the volume you run, this page answers that instead.

Is this page affiliated with Crest Capital?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Crest Capital. Crest Capital is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not.

This page is a factual comparison of what each tool does, not an evaluation of which is better. Details about Crest Capital above describe the general shape of its business and calculator as publicly described at the time of writing and may have changed — verify against Crest Capital's own site before deciding, and no specific rate, fee, or price for Crest Capital's financing is stated here.
